title: The Particle-Wave Duality
lead: EM radiation interferes like a wave and interacts as discrete photons like a particle. This section explains what the words wave and particle mean for things too small to see, names this twofold nature the particle-wave duality, and asks whether matter has wave properties too.
objectives: Explain what the term particle-wave duality means, and why it is applied to EM radiation.
summary_html:
• EM radiation can behave like either a particle or a wave.
  • This is termed particle-wave duality.

exercises.prompt: The ground state of a certain type of atom has energy of –E0. What is the wavelength of a photon with enough energy to ionize the atom when it is in the ground state, so that the ejected electron has kinetic energy equal to 2E0?

answer.hint: The photon must supply $E_{0}$ to free the electron and $2E_{0}$ more as its kinetic energy; then use $E = hc/\lambda$.

exercises.prompt: While the quantum model explains many physical processes that the classical model cannot, it must be consistent with those processes that the classical model does explain. Energy and momentum conservation are fundamental principles of classical physics. Use the Compton and photoelectric effects to explain how these conservation principles carry over to the quantum model of light.

answer.solution: In the photoelectric effect a single photon gives all its energy $hf$ to one electron. Part of that energy frees the electron from the material, and the rest becomes the electron’s kinetic energy, so $\text{KE}_e = hf - \text{BE}$ is a statement that energy is conserved photon by photon. In the Compton effect a photon collides with an electron as one particle collides with another. The scattered photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength, the electron recoils, and the momentum of the photon before the collision equals the vector sum of the scattered photon’s momentum and the electron’s momentum after it. The classical principles are unchanged; what the quantum model adds is that light carries its energy and momentum in discrete amounts, $hf$ and $h/\lambda$, which are exchanged whole in each interaction.
